Q001718.stem: A startup needs encrypted connectivity from its office to a VPC this week, with about 200 Mbps of unpredictable traffic, while it evaluates Direct Connect over the next quarter. Which option fits, and what is its main limitation?

choices.text: Site-to-Site VPN; each tunnel tops out around 1.25 Gbps
VPC peering to the office network over the internet
A dedicated 10 Gbps Direct Connect port, which is always cheaper than VPN
A hosted Direct Connect connection, which encrypts traffic by default

Q001718.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Site-to-Site VPN is IPsec-encrypted, can be set up in minutes with no long-term commitment, and easily carries 200 Mbps. Its main limit is per-tunnel throughput (about 1.25 Gbps) over the variable internet path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated 10 Gbps DX: takes weeks to provision, and port hours are costly for 200 Mbps.
• Hosted DX: not encrypted by default, and provisioning takes time through a partner.
• VPC peering: connects VPCs only, not on-premises networks.

Key takeaway: fast, encrypted, low commitment → VPN; consistent high bandwidth → Direct Connect.

Q001737.stem: A company has Shield Advanced on an internet-facing ALB and wants automatic application-layer DDoS mitigation, with rules created and removed during attacks without manual work. What is required?

choices.text: Put the ALB behind CloudFront, since automatic L7 mitigation works only there
Associate a WAF web ACL with the ALB and enable automatic mitigation
Use a fixed target group without Auto Scaling
Disable AWS WAF, since Shield Advanced replaces its rule engine

Q001737.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced's automatic application layer mitigation places rules in a WAF web ACL associated with the protected resource. Without a web ACL on the ALB, it has nowhere to put mitigation rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront only: ALBs are supported when a web ACL is associated.
• Disabling WAF: removes the mechanism mitigation depends on.
• Fixed target group: unrelated to mitigation.

Key takeaway: Shield Advanced L7 auto-mitigation = rules inside your WAF web ACL.

Q001589.stem: A public app runs on an ALB in eu-central-1 without CloudFront. Security must block SQL injection and rate-limit IPs, and the web ACL must be managed centrally by Firewall Manager. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Shield Advanced alone, which includes SQLi managed rules
A CLOUDFRONT-scoped web ACL in us-east-1 associated with the ALB
A web ACL associated with the VPC route table
A REGIONAL web ACL in eu-central-1 on the ALB, via Firewall Manager

Q001589.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALBs use REGIONAL web ACLs in their own Region. Firewall Manager policies can deploy and enforce WAF web ACLs on in-scope ALBs across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CLOUDFRONT scope: only for CloudFront distributions.
• Route tables: WAF associates with resources, not route tables.
• Shield Advanced alone: DDoS protection, not SQLi rules.

Key takeaway: ALB WAF = REGIONAL in its Region.

Q001594.stem: A CloudFront distribution serves only North American and European customers. The company wants to cut costs without blocking anyone. Which setting fits, and what is the trade-off?

choices.text: A Price Class that excludes other regions; distant viewers get higher latency
A shorter TTL to reduce edge usage
Geo restriction allowing only North America and Europe, blocking all other viewers
Origin Shield in South America

Q001594.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Price classes limit which edge locations serve content, lowering cost. Viewers elsewhere are still served, from the nearest included edge, with higher latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Geo restriction: blocks users, which isn't wanted.
• Shorter TTL: increases origin fetches and cost.
• Origin Shield: adds a caching layer, not an edge limit.

Key takeaway: cheaper edges without blocking → Price Class.

Q001596.stem: A team wants to send 5% of production traffic to a new backend, then 25%, then 100%, with the ability to roll back instantly, using DNS. Which Route 53 setup fits, and what limits rollback speed?

choices.text: Failover records with the new version as secondary, promoted by health checks
Latency records per version
Geolocation records by continent
Weighted records with health checks; DNS TTL caching slows shifts

Q001596.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing splits DNS answers by weight, so changing weights shifts traffic. Resolver caching of the TTL delays how fast changes take effect, so use low TTLs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency: routes by performance, not by percentage.
• Failover: all-or-nothing.
• Geolocation: splits by location, not percentage.

Key takeaway: percentage shifts in DNS → weighted records; keep TTLs low.

Q001603.stem: A team needs DNS load balancing across 8 web server IPs, with unhealthy IPs removed automatically, and clients receiving several IPs per answer. No load balancer is allowed. Which routing fits?

choices.text: Simple routing with one record holding 8 IPs
Multivalue answer with a health check per record
Weighted routing with equal weights and a health check on each record
Latency routing across the 8 records

Q001603.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multivalue answer returns up to 8 healthy records per query and omits records whose health checks fail, providing basic DNS-level load distribution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Simple routing: returns all values with no health checking.
• Weighted: returns one record per query.
• Latency: routes by Region, not across 8 servers.

Key takeaway: multiple healthy IPs per answer → multivalue.

Q001610.stem: A shopping app behind an ALB must keep users on the same target for 30 minutes. The app already issues its own session cookie named SESSIONID. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Duration-based stickiness, since ALB can't use app cookies
Source-IP stickiness on the target group
Stickiness is only available on NLB
Application-based stickiness using the SESSIONID cookie

Q001610.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB supports application-based cookie stickiness, where it follows a cookie your application sets (and uses AWSALBAPP), as well as duration-based stickiness with its own AWSALB cookie.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Duration-based only: ALB also supports application cookies.
• Source-IP: NLB feature, not ALB.
• NLB only: ALB supports stickiness.

Key takeaway: reuse the app's cookie → application-based stickiness.

Q001612.stem: A partner must allow-list a small fixed set of IPs for your internet-facing endpoint, and you also need TLS termination with ACM and path routing. Which design fits?

choices.text: An ALB with Elastic IPs assigned per AZ
NLB with Elastic IPs in front of an ALB target
A Gateway Load Balancer with static IPs
A Classic Load Balancer with fixed IPs

Q001612.explanation:
Why this is correct:
NLBs support one static or Elastic IP per AZ. An ALB can be registered as an NLB target, combining fixed IPs with ALB features such as path routing (TLS can terminate on the ALB with ACM).

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB with EIPs: ALBs don't support Elastic IPs.
• GWLB: for appliances.
• CLB: no static IPs.

Key takeaway: static IPs + L7 features → NLB in front of ALB (or Global Accelerator).

Q001613.stem: One ALB serves api.example.com and www.example.com. The certificate must cover both names, and routing must split by name. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Path rules on /api and /www prefixes
Query-string rules to identify the site
Host-header rules plus SNI with a certificate per name
Two ALBs, one per domain name, sharing one wildcard certificate

Q001613.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Host-based rules route by the Host header, and ALB HTTPS listeners support multiple certificates with SNI, or one certificate covering both names.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Path rules: the names differ, not the paths.
• Two ALBs: unnecessary cost.
• Query strings: not how clients distinguish sites.

Key takeaway: name-based routing → host-header rules + SNI.

Q001620.stem: Security wants flow logs for every ENI in a VPC, including ENIs created later by Lambda and load balancers, with custom fields including pkt-srcaddr. What should be configured?

choices.text: Subnet-level flow logs for existing subnets only
One VPC-level flow log with a custom format
CloudTrail data events for EC2
Per-ENI flow logs added by an EventBridge rule

Q001620.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A VPC-level flow log covers all current and future ENIs in the VPC, and custom formats can include fields such as pkt-srcaddr.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-ENI automation: fragile and unnecessary.
• Existing subnets only: misses new subnets.
• CloudTrail: logs API calls, not traffic.

Key takeaway: broadest coverage → VPC-level flow logs.

Q001625.stem: A company wants to bundle two 10 Gbps dedicated connections into one 20 Gbps logical link and keep it up if one fails. Which option fits, and what are the constraints?

choices.text: A Transit Gateway Connect attachment
Two private VIFs advertising the same prefixes with equal BGP weights for ECMP
A Direct Connect gateway joining the two connections
A LAG: same speed, same DX endpoint; set minimum links

Q001625.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A link aggregation group (LAG) combines dedicated connections of the same bandwidth terminating on the same AWS device into one logical interface. The minimum-links setting controls when the LAG stays operational.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX gateway: connects to VPCs and TGWs; doesn't aggregate links.
• TGW Connect: GRE tunnels for SD-WAN.
• Two VIFs with ECMP-like weights: not a single logical link, and failure behavior differs.

Key takeaway: bundle physical links → LAG (same speed, same device).

Q001633.stem: A company needs Direct Connect quickly, doesn't want to manage a cross-connect or port, and needs only 500 Mbps. Which option fits, and what does it give up?

choices.text: A partner hosted connection; no LAG or MACsec
A Site-to-Site VPN over a public VIF
A hosted VIF shared from another company's port
A dedicated 1 Gbps connection, which offers the same features

Q001633.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Partner hosted connections come in speeds such as 500 Mbps, with the partner handling physical connectivity. LAGs and MACsec require dedicated connections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated 1 Gbps: involves a cross-connect and port management.
• Hosted VIF: a virtual interface on someone else's connection, with shared capacity.
• VPN over a public VIF: still needs a DX connection.

Key takeaway: sub-1 Gbps, fast, managed → hosted connection.

Q001636.stem: An architect is comparing VPC peering with Transit Gateway for 60 VPCs. Which TWO statements about peering are correct? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Peering isn't transitive: A-B and B-C doesn't give A-C
Peering can't be used across accounts
Each VPC has a quota on active peering connections
Peering can't be used across Regions
Peering charges an hourly fee per peering attachment, like Transit Gateway

Q001636.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Peering creates direct one-to-one connections and doesn't route through an intermediary VPC, and each VPC has a limit on active peerings, so a full mesh of 60 VPCs becomes unmanageable. Transit Gateway gives hub-and-spoke routing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hourly attachment fee: that's a Transit Gateway charge; peering has no hourly fee.
• Cross-account and cross-Region: both are supported by peering.

Key takeaway: many VPCs → Transit Gateway; a few with heavy traffic → peering can be cheaper.

Q001643.stem: A network account owns a Transit Gateway that 30 accounts must attach to, and attachments should be accepted automatically only from the organization. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Copy the TGW configuration into each account with StackSets
Share via RAM within the org; accounts create attachments
Create all attachments centrally by assuming roles into each account
Enable a TGW delegated administrator to attach all VPCs

Q001643.explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS RAM shares the TGW with the organization, so member accounts can create their own VPC attachments. The owner can enable auto-accept for shared attachments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Central attachments via roles: heavy and centralizes work unnecessarily.
• Copying config: creates separate TGWs.
• Delegated admin auto-attach: not how TGW sharing works.

Key takeaway: shared network resources → RAM.

Q001644.stem: A company wants MACsec on a new Direct Connect link later. Which choices at provisioning time keep this option open?

choices.text: A 1 Gbps dedicated connection at any location, upgraded to MACsec later
Any hosted connection, then enable MACsec later
MACsec is enabled automatically on LAGs
Dedicated 10/100/400 Gbps at a MACsec-capable location

Q001644.explanation:
Why this is correct:
MACsec is supported on dedicated connections at eligible speeds (10, 100, 400 Gbps) on MACsec-capable devices, so these choices must be made at order time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hosted connections: don't support MACsec.
• 1 Gbps: not an eligible speed.
• Automatic on LAGs: it must be configured with keys.

Key takeaway: MACsec = dedicated + eligible speed + capable location.

Q001651.stem: A branch router doesn't support BGP. It connects with Site-to-Site VPN to a VGW. What must be configured, and how does failover between the two tunnels work?

choices.text: Static routes; failover depends on the device detecting tunnel state
Policy-based VPN, since routing options don't apply
Static routing, with AWS failing over automatically via BGP withdrawal
BGP, since static routing isn't supported

Q001651.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Without BGP, the VPN uses static routes that list on-premises prefixes. There's no route withdrawal, so the customer device must detect a down tunnel (for example, with DPD) and use the other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BGP required: static routing is supported.
• Automatic BGP withdrawal: there's no BGP.
• Policy-based only: static routing still applies.

Key takeaway: static VPN = manual prefixes + device-driven failover.

Q001670.stem: VPCs must resolve corp.example.internal via on-premises DNS over Direct Connect, and on-premises must resolve a private hosted zone. Which components fit?

choices.text: No endpoints; DNS flows over the VPN automatically
A public hosted zone with NS records to on-premises
Outbound endpoint + forwarding rule; inbound endpoint for on-prem
An inbound endpoint only, with a private hosted zone

Q001670.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Outbound endpoints with forwarding rules send VPC queries for on-premises domains to on-premises DNS. Inbound endpoints receive queries from on-premises for private hosted zones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inbound only: covers on-prem-to-AWS but not the reverse.
• Public zone: exposes internal names.
• Automatic flow: the VPC resolver doesn't forward on its own.

Key takeaway: AWS → on-prem = outbound; on-prem → AWS = inbound.

Q001677.stem: Instances must not resolve malware C2 domains, using AWS-maintained lists, while a partner domain wrongly flagged must stay allowed. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: NACLs denying the IP ranges published for known C2 infrastructure
DNS Firewall: ALLOW rule for the partner first, then managed BLOCK list
Security groups blocking outbound port 53
GuardDuty DNS findings as the blocking mechanism

Q001677.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall evaluates rules by priority. A higher-priority ALLOW rule for the partner domain, followed by a BLOCK rule using the AWS managed malware list, handles the exception.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG port 53: blocks all DNS, not specific domains.
• NACL IP ranges: C2 IPs change; not domain-based.
• GuardDuty: detects, doesn't block.

Key takeaway: domain blocking with exceptions → DNS Firewall rule priority.

Q001679.stem: A network team must deploy the same Transit Gateway route tables and VPC attachments to 40 accounts and 3 Regions, with drift detection. Which approach fits?

choices.text: EventBridge schedules calling EC2 APIs
Manual console setup with a runbook
AWS Config rules that create missing resources
CloudFormation StackSets with TGW resource types

Q001679.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFormation declares TGW resources such as route tables, attachments, and associations, and StackSets deploys them across accounts and Regions, with drift detection on stack instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config rules: evaluate compliance, not provisioning.
• Scheduled API scripts: imperative, with no drift detection.
• Manual setup: inconsistent at this scale.

Key takeaway: multi-account IaC → StackSets.

Q001683.stem: The NOC wants one topology view of TGWs in 4 Regions, on-premises sites, SD-WAN devices, and link health, plus route analysis between two endpoints. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Config advanced queries
AWS Network Manager with a global network and Route Analyzer
Trusted Advisor network checks
CloudWatch Synthetics canaries probing each site and Region

Q001683.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Manager provides a global network view that registers TGWs, sites, devices, and links, visualizes topology and health, and its Route Analyzer checks paths between endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config queries: resource configuration, with no topology view.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.
• Synthetics: endpoint tests, not topology.

Key takeaway: global network topology → Network Manager.

Q001689.stem: The NOC needs a safe, auditable procedure to reset a DX BGP session: check health, require approval, act, and verify, run by humans or by an alarm. Which fits?

choices.text: An SSM Automation runbook with an approval step
A Lambda function with a sleep for approval
A CloudWatch alarm action that resets BGP
An AWS Config remediation action that runs without any approval step

Q001689.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automation runbooks define multi-step procedures, including aws:approve steps, API actions, and checks, with execution history for audit. They can be started manually or by EventBridge.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda sleeping: time-limited and not auditable as a procedure.
• Config remediation: no approval here, and not suited to this operation.
• Alarm actions: limited to specific actions such as SNS or Auto Scaling.

Key takeaway: auditable, gated operations → Automation runbooks.

Q001695.stem: A VPN has two tunnels. The NOC wants a page when either tunnel is down for 2 minutes, and a separate critical page when both are down. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Alarms on TunnelState per tunnel, plus a composite alarm
An alarm on the Direct Connect ConnectionState metric for the link
An alarm on EC2 NetworkPacketsIn
An alarm on TGW BytesIn for the attachment

Q001695.explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS/VPN publishes TunnelState per tunnel (1 up, 0 down). A per-tunnel alarm catches single failures, and a composite alarm (AND) catches total loss.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX metric: Direct Connect, not VPN.
• TGW bytes: low traffic isn't the same as a down tunnel.
• EC2 packets: unrelated.

Key takeaway: VPN health → TunnelState; combine with composite alarms.

Q001706.stem: Before a change window, an engineer wants to prove, without sending traffic, whether an instance can reach an RDS endpoint in another VPC via TGW, and which component would block it. Which tool fits?

choices.text: Traffic Mirroring
CloudWatch Network Monitor probes between the endpoints
VPC Reachability Analyzer
VPC Flow Logs

Q001706.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reachability Analyzer performs static analysis of configuration (routes, security groups, NACLs, TGW) between a source and destination, and names the blocking component, without sending packets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: show traffic that actually occurred.
• Traffic Mirroring: copies real packets.
• Network Monitor: measures real loss and latency with probes.

Key takeaway: 'would it work?' without traffic → Reachability Analyzer.

Q001712.stem: Traffic Mirroring fails for a source ENI on an older instance type. What is the cause, and what fixes it?

choices.text: The source isn't Nitro-based; move to a Nitro instance type
Only one mirror session is allowed per VPC
The mirror target must be created first
The source ENI must be in a public subnet with an internet gateway route

Q001712.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Traffic Mirroring requires sources on Nitro-based instance types. Changing the instance to a supported Nitro type resolves it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One session per VPC: not a restriction.
• Public subnet: not required.
• Target first: order isn't the issue.

Key takeaway: Traffic Mirroring = Nitro sources.

Q001736.stem: A customer asks how WAF and Shield Advanced differ for an API under both SQL injection attempts and volumetric DDoS. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: WAF filters L7 requests; Shield Advanced adds DDoS defense and support
Shield Advanced replaces WAF by blocking malicious payloads without rules
Both work only at Layer 3/4
WAF must be bought with Shield Advanced

Q001736.explanation:
Why this is correct:
WAF inspects HTTP requests (SQL injection, rate limits). Shield Advanced adds enhanced DDoS detection and mitigation (including L7 with a web ACL), the Shield Response Team, and cost protection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• L3/4 only: WAF is L7.
• Bundled purchase: WAF is standalone (Shield Advanced includes WAF usage for protected resources, but WAF doesn't require it).
• Replaces WAF: Shield uses WAF for L7 mitigation.

Key takeaway: WAF = request filtering; Shield Advanced = DDoS resilience + support.

Q001741.stem: An app tier accepts traffic only from a web tier. Both scale dynamically across 3 AZs, and IPs change constantly. Which rule fits?

choices.text: Reference the web SG ID in the app subnet's NACL
App SG inbound: allow the web tier's security group
Add each web instance IP as a /32 rule
Allow the whole VPC CIDR in the app tier SG

Q001741.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security group references allow traffic from any ENI in the referenced group, regardless of IP, so scaling needs no rule changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Whole VPC CIDR: too broad.
• NACL SG reference: NACLs can't reference security groups.
• /32 per instance: breaks with scaling and hits rule limits.

Key takeaway: reference security groups, not IPs.

Q001747.stem: An auditor asks whether AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress and CreateVpc calls are captured by a trail with default settings, and for how long they're queryable without a trail. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: Neither is logged unless data events are enabled
Only CreateVpc is logged by default; security group changes need data events
Both are management events; event history keeps 90 days
VPC API calls appear only in VPC Flow Logs

Q001747.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Both calls change resource configuration, so they are management events logged by default. CloudTrail event history shows 90 days of management events even without a trail; a trail stores them long-term.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data events: those are object- or item-level operations.
• Only CreateVpc: both are management events.
• Flow logs: capture traffic, not API calls.

Key takeaway: configuration changes = management events.

Q001750.stem: The compliance team wants continuous evaluation of security groups for SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0, with automatic removal of the bad rule across the organization. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector network reachability findings reviewed each week
restricted-ssh via conformance pack, with SSM remediation
Trusted Advisor cost checks
CloudTrail Insights on security group changes

Q001750.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The managed Config rule restricted-ssh evaluates security groups continuously. Deployed org-wide (for example, in a conformance pack) with automatic remediation via an SSM document, it removes the offending rule.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector reachability: assessment, not continuous compliance with remediation.
• Trusted Advisor cost checks: wrong category.
• CloudTrail Insights: anomaly detection.

Key takeaway: continuous config compliance + fix → Config rule + remediation.

Q001753.stem: Requirement 1: verify VPC configurations against internal rules continuously. Requirement 2: detect instances communicating with known malicious IPs. Which pairing fits?

choices.text: Security Hub alone for both, with no other service
GuardDuty for requirement 1; Config for requirement 2
Config for both, with custom rules on traffic
Config for requirement 1; GuardDuty for requirement 2

Q001753.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Config evaluates resource configuration against rules. GuardDuty analyzes VPC traffic, DNS, and CloudTrail data against threat intelligence to detect malicious activity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: each service in the other's role.
• Config for traffic: Config doesn't analyze traffic.
• Security Hub alone: aggregates findings; it relies on services like Config and GuardDuty.

Key takeaway: configuration → Config; behavior and threats → GuardDuty.

Q001754.stem: GuardDuty reports UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/MaliciousIPCaller for an instance. What does it indicate, and what is a sound first response?

choices.text: An IAM user signed in from a Tor exit node
WAF blocked a malicious HTTP request to it
Its security group was changed by an unauthorized user
It is talking to a threat-listed IP; isolate and investigate

Q001754.explanation:
Why this is correct:
This finding means the instance is communicating with an IP on a threat intelligence list. Isolate it (for example, swap to a restrictive security group), preserve evidence, and investigate with Detective.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG changed: that would appear as a different finding or event type.
• WAF block: not a GuardDuty finding.
• Tor sign-in: a different IAM-related finding.

Key takeaway: read the finding type to know what was observed, then contain and preserve evidence.

Q001758.stem: A VPN connection has two tunnels. The customer device keeps only tunnel 1 up, and during AWS maintenance traffic dropped. What should the customer do?

choices.text: Configure both tunnels (BGP preferred) so one takes over
Configure only tunnel 2 as a manual backup that the NOC brings up
Use the second tunnel for IPv6 only
Request that AWS skip maintenance on tunnel 1

Q001758.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The two tunnels terminate on different AWS endpoints for redundancy. AWS may take one tunnel down for maintenance, so both must be configured, ideally with BGP, so traffic fails over automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual backup: slow and error-prone.
• IPv6-only tunnel: not the purpose of the second tunnel.
• Skipping maintenance: not an option.

Key takeaway: always configure both VPN tunnels.
